source: Cobbe et al. (2021) Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems
finding: A learned verifier that ranks 100 sampled solutions beats fine-tuning alone on GSM8K. The gain grows with training data size.
numbers: Verifier gave about the same boost as a 30x larger model (paper's claim). 6B fine-tuned model forced to answer with no reasoning text: 20.6% falls to 5.2%. Ranked 100 test completions per problem; verification did not help at small training sets.
quote: approximately the same performance boost as a 30x model size increase
limits: Verifier trained on final-answer labels only, so some positives had flawed reasoning (false positives). Overfitting hurts small data. Dropout was a strong regularizer.
agent_relevance: Verifiers need enough labelled data to pay off. Do not train a verifier on a small set; use a code check where one exists.

source: Cobbe et al. (2021) verifier ablations: number of candidates and token-level scoring
finding: Token-level verifier scores beat solution-level scores late in training. Test accuracy as a function of candidates per problem was checked from 25 to 3200 (Fig 6a); training jointly with a language-model objective was a strict improvement (Fig 6b).
numbers: 6B verifier, GSM8K, 25 to 3200 completions per test problem.
limits: Exact peak values only seen in plots, not read as numbers. GSM8K only.
agent_relevance: Cap the number of candidates a learned verifier ranks; more samples give the verifier more chances to pick a fluent wrong answer.

source: Uesato et al. (2022) Solving math word problems with process- and outcome-based feedback
finding: Outcome supervision gives about the same final-answer accuracy as process supervision on GSM8K, but process supervision gives far fewer bad reasoning traces.
numbers: Final-answer error 16.8% to 12.7%; trace error 14.0% to 3.4% (best). With abstention on 30% of questions, final-answer error 2.7%. SFT vs final-answer RL: 22.3% vs 23.5% without a reward model, 14.8% vs 16.6% with an ORM. Final-answer RL had trace error 12.4% versus 5.5% when reranked by a reward model.
limits: GSM8K only. Trace correctness judged by human annotators on small samples.
agent_relevance: If only the answer matters, an outcome check is enough. If the reasoning will be read or reused, an answer check hides wrong reasoning behind right answers.

source: Lightman et al. (2023) Let's Verify Step by Step
finding: Step-level human labels (PRM800K) train a better verifier than outcome labels. Best-of-N with the process reward model solved 78.2% of a MATH test subset.
numbers: Best-of-1860 with PRM: 78.2% (ORM 72.4%). Out-of-distribution STEM test, 234 problems: PRM 72.9%, ORM 63.8%, majority vote 61.3% (AP Calc 86.7/68.9/80.0; AP Physics 86.7/77.8/82.2; AMC10/12 53.2/49.1/32.8, as PRM/ORM/vote).
limits: Large generator and 800K human step labels; MATH is the main test. Later work (c11, c12) finds open PRMs do not transfer to harder sets.
agent_relevance: A step-aware verifier helps most with many samples and long chains. Majority vote is a strong baseline; PRM beats it by about 3 to 11 points here.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: With a perfect verifier, repeated sampling raises coverage log-linearly over four orders of magnitude. Common selectors (majority vote, reward model) stop gaining after a few hundred samples.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 samples (prior single-attempt SOTA 43%). CodeContests Gemma-2B: 0.02% to 7.1% at 10,000 samples. MATH Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000, while vote or reward model go only 40.50% to 41.41%.
quote: coverage increases from 82.9% with 100 samples to 98.44% with 10,000 samples
limits: Coverage counts only with an automatic verifier. Selection methods saturate before 100 samples.
agent_relevance: The gap is the point: generation reaches 98% but selection stays near 41%. The verifier, not the sampler, is the bottleneck on tasks with no executable check.

source: Brown et al. (2024) verifier imperfection: flaky tests, false negatives, and are answer-only checks lucky guesses
finding: Even code unit tests are imperfect verifiers. Some correct answers fail, some wrong ones pass. For GSM8K, answer checks mostly mark faithful reasoning.
numbers: 11.3% of SWE-bench Lite problems have flaky test suites that sometimes fail even the gold patch. CodeContests has false-negative tests when several outputs are valid. Manual check of 105 correct GSM8K chains from Llama-3-8B-Instruct: over 90% were faithful.
limits: Small manual sample (105). Flaky-test finding is for one benchmark.
agent_relevance: Run tests several times and use a majority for flaky ones. Treat a pass as a strong hint, not proof (G3).

source: Stroebl, Kapoor, Narayanan (2024, v3 2026) The Limits of Inference Scaling Through Resampling
finding: With an imperfect verifier (unit tests), resampling has a ceiling and then loses value: weaker models make false positives at higher rates, so infinite samples cannot match a strong model.
numbers: HumanEval+ and MBPP+ tested with the smaller original tests as verifier. False-positive rate rises with attempts K. With a cost on false positives the optimal K is finite and low; in their fitted model even at zero compute cost the optimum is about K of 3 or less (Fig 13). 28 tasks excluded for oracle issues.
quote: even if given an infinite inference budget, in many cases a weaker model cannot match
limits: Coding only; theory claimed domain-agnostic. The cost-benefit ratio is a modelling choice.
agent_relevance: Set number of tries by verifier precision. A weak verifier plus many samples selects plausible but wrong answers. Prefer held-out tests (G3).

source: Stroebl et al. false positives are lower-quality code
finding: Solutions that pass the weak tests but fail the extended ones also score worse on code quality metrics.
numbers: Naming convention, line length and other readability metrics are worse for false positives than for robust solutions across all models (Fig 7, Fig 16). Qualitative review of 10 false positives per benchmark: mostly logic errors and edge cases, some inefficiency.
limits: Qualitative sample is small.
agent_relevance: Cheap static checks may add a weak secondary signal on top of tests.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: The best verifier strategy depends on question difficulty. Beam search against a PRM wins on hard questions at low budget; best-of-N wins on easy questions and high budget. Choosing by difficulty beats uniform best-of-N.
numbers: Compute-optimal allocation beats best-of-N with up to 4x less test-time compute (e.g. 16 vs 64 generations). The paper reports PaLM 2-S* with test-time compute beating a 14x larger model run once on easy and medium questions.
quote: outperform best-of-N using up to 4x less test-time compute
limits: MATH with PaLM 2 models fine-tuned for revision and verification; difficulty estimated by model pass rate (two-fold cross-validation). Benefit shrinks when difficulty is predicted rather than oracle.
agent_relevance: Supports G12: spend by difficulty. Use verifier search on harder items, plain sampling on easy ones.

source: Zhang et al. (2024/2025) Generative Verifiers: Reward Modeling as Next-Token Prediction (GenRM)
finding: A verifier trained to write a verification chain of thought and then judge beats a discriminative scorer, a DPO verifier and a prompted judge, and gains more with a vote over several verifications.
numbers: Best-of-N: algorithmic tasks 5% to 45.3%, GSM8K 73% to 93.4%; easy-to-hard transfer MATH 28% to 44.6%, MMLU abstract algebra 37.9% to 53.5%. Gemma2-9B verifiers; the prompted judge baseline is Gemini 1.0 Pro. Fig reports needing about 2.5x fewer solutions than the discriminative RM.
limits: Verifiers trained on synthetic rationales; baseline judge was not the strongest available. GSM8K-level math.
agent_relevance: Sampling k short verification chains and voting in code is a workable S8 VERIFY when training is not possible.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Existing open process reward models do not generalise to hard problems. Prompted general models used as critics beat them. Finding the first wrong step is hard.
numbers: 3,400 cases with expert error-step labels. Average F1 printed in the figure: o1-mini 87.9, QwQ-32B-Preview 71.5, GPT-4o 61.9. Math-Shepherd-PRM-7B F1: GSM8K 47.9, MATH 29.5, OlympiadBench 24.8. Their Qwen2.5-Math-7B-PRM800K: 68.2, 62.6, 50.7.
quote: Existing PRMs typically fail to generalize to more challenging math problems
limits: Extracted table columns were garbled; only numbers tied to a clear label are quoted. Math only.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on step models trained on easy data for hard problems; a strong reasoning model as critic is the better verifier.

source: Yuan et al. (2024) Free Process Rewards without Process Labels
finding: An outcome-trained reward model can give step-level scores if its reward is parameterised as a log-likelihood ratio, with no step labels.
numbers: Beat a Math-Shepherd-style MCTS baseline using under 1/38 of the training data on MATH; works with one response per instruction (CE loss); majority vote adds more.
limits: MATH only; best-of-N reranking.
agent_relevance: Step-level signal can be cheap. Test this before paying for step labels.

source: Khalifa et al. (2025) Process Reward Models That Think (ThinkPRM)
finding: A long-chain-of-thought verifier fine-tuned on about 1% of PRM800K labels beats LLM-as-a-judge and a discriminative PRM, and scales better with verification tokens.
numbers: Out-of-domain: +8% on a GPQA-Diamond subset and +4.5% on a LiveCodeBench subset over a discriminative PRM trained on full PRM800K. At equal token budget +7.2% over LLM-as-a-Judge on a ProcessBench subset.
limits: Subsets, not full benchmarks. Numbers taken from abstract and intro.
agent_relevance: Generative verification with extra tokens is worth its cost; a prompted judge is the weak baseline.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
finding: LLM judges agree with humans over 80% (same as human-human) but show position, verbosity and self-enhancement bias and weak math grading.
numbers: Position consistency after swapping order: GPT-4 65.0%, GPT-3.5 46.2%, Claude-v1 23.8% (Claude favoured first position 75.0%). Few-shot prompt raised GPT-4 consistency 65.0% to 77.5% at 4x cost. Repetitive-list attack failure: Claude-v1 91.3%, GPT-3.5 91.3%, GPT-4 8.7% (23 answers). Judge wrongly approved wrong math answers in 14/20 with default prompt, 6/20 with CoT, 3/20 with reference answer.
quote: achieving over 80% agreement, the same level of agreement between humans
limits: Small samples (80 questions for position, 10 math questions). Older models.
agent_relevance: Judge both orders and keep only consistent wins. Give the judge a reference answer or tool output when one exists.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators
finding: Swapping response order alone can flip the winner. Three fixes: several evidence chains, balanced position averaging, and human help on high-entropy cases.
numbers: Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries when ChatGPT was the evaluator and ordering favoured Vicuna.
limits: Single benchmark of 80 queries.
agent_relevance: Position-balanced scoring in code is cheap and needed for any pairwise judge step.

source: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng (2024) LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
finding: Models can tell their own text from others better than chance, and the strength of self-preference rises linearly with self-recognition.
numbers: GPT-4 distinguishes itself from another source 73.5% of the time out of the box; GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 over 90% after fine-tuning on 500 examples. Pairwise order-flip rates: GPT-4 25%, GPT-3.5 58%, Llama 89%.
limits: Summarization tasks (CNN/DailyMail, XSum); causal link shown by fine-tuning, not in natural models.
agent_relevance: Hide authorship from the judge (G5) and prefer a different model family as judge.

source: Wataoka et al. (2024/2025) Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
finding: Judges favour text with low perplexity (familiar to them), whether or not they wrote it. Self-preference is largely a familiarity effect.
numbers: GPT-4 shows significant self-preference by their new metric; judges score low-perplexity outputs higher than humans do.
limits: Effect sizes not extracted. Dialogue evaluation only.
agent_relevance: Rewrites by the same model and generic phrasing will be over-rated. Use external checks for anything the same model family produced.

source: Huang et al. (2023) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without outside feedback, asking a model to review and fix its answer leaves reasoning accuracy equal or worse.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7 over two rounds; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8. 74.7% of GPT-3.5 GSM8K cases kept the first answer; more changes went right-to-wrong than wrong-to-right.
limits: Earlier positive results used oracle labels to decide when to stop.
agent_relevance: Matches G2: revise only from real output. A self-judging loop with no tool is a net loss.

source: Stechly, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong
finding: On graph colouring GPT-4 is no better at verifying than solving. Self-critique is worse than no loop. A sound external verifier helps, but richer feedback adds almost nothing.
numbers: 100 instances, 10 to 17 nodes. Baseline 16%. With the LLM as its own verifier only 1 of 100 correct. In 40 instances the generator produced a correct colouring at some point and the LLM verifier never accepted it; in 39 it invented same-colour adjacent vertices. With a sound verifier near 40%; pass/fail feedback about as good as full error lists. Sampling 15 candidates at t=1.0 matched backprompting at about 40%.
limits: One NP-complete task and one model.
agent_relevance: Tests the claim that verifying is easier than generating. For LLM self-verification it failed here. Resampling matched backprompting.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Mistake finding is the weak step of self-correction, not fixing. With the true mistake location, backtracking helps; a random location helps much less.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2,186 PaLM 2 Unicorn CoT traces, 300 sampled per task with 85% wrong-answer traces, first error labelled. Word sorting with oracle location: 11.11% of correct traces turned wrong, 23.53% of incorrect traces turned right. A small classifier trained on out-of-domain data beat a prompted large model on mistake finding (gains on 4 of 5 tasks). Prompted trace-level F1 is near the trivial 78 baseline.
limits: Five tasks, one generator.
agent_relevance: Supports G2: code or tests must say where it failed, then the model fixes it.

source: Chen et al. (2022) CodeT: Code Generation with Generated Tests
finding: Having the model write its own unit tests and picking the solution that agrees most with tests and with other solutions (dual execution agreement) raises code pass rates.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 with code-davinci-002 reached 65.8%, +18.8% absolute. Tested on 5 models and 4 benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, APPS, CodeContests).
limits: Generated tests share the generator's blind spots, so errors correlate (G4). Needs executable problems.
agent_relevance: A ready-made S4 TEST design. Use generated tests with execution and keep them independent of the answer.

source: Gao, Schulman, Hilton (2022) Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
finding: Optimising against a learned reward model first raises then lowers the true reward. The best-of-n curve follows a simple fitted form.
numbers: Best-of-n: R(d) = d(alpha - beta*d); RL: R(d) = d(alpha - beta*log d), d the square root of KL. Coefficients vary smoothly with reward model size. Policy size matters little for overoptimisation. A KL penalty raised the proxy score but not the gold score.
limits: Synthetic gold reward model used as ground truth. Best-of-n on chat tasks, not reasoning.
agent_relevance: Best-of-N against any learned verifier degrades past a point. Keep N moderate and add checks the verifier did not see.

source: Setlur et al. (2025) Scaling Test-Time Compute Without Verification or RL is Suboptimal
finding: Proof and experiments show verifier-based methods (RL or search) beat verifier-free distillation, with a gap that widens as the test-time budget grows.
numbers: Experiments with 3B, 8B and 32B models; compares s1-style distillation with best-of-N search.
limits: Needs a wide spread of correct traces and a non-sharp reward distribution (anti-concentration). Fine-tuned settings.
agent_relevance: Verification matters more as test-time spend grows. Spend part of the budget on verification.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Instruction-Following Evaluation for Large Language Models (IFEval)
finding: A benchmark where every prompt has constraints that code can check, avoiding LLM judges.
numbers: Deterministic scripts score strict and loose accuracy. Prompt counts not re-verified here.
limits: Only checks constraints that code can test, not content quality.
agent_relevance: Model for tasks that can be verified by code: turn the requirement into a checker before generating.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Math-Shepherd
finding: Automatic step labels from Monte Carlo rollouts can train a PRM without humans. Known from the ProcessBench and Yuan comparisons, not read directly.
numbers: Not read this session; no numbers quoted here.
limits: Unverified; ProcessBench shows weak transfer (c11).
agent_relevance: Cheap step labels are possible but unreliable on hard problems.

source: Saad-Falcon et al. (2025) Weaver: Shrinking the Generation-Verification Gap with Weak Verifiers
finding: Combining many weak verifiers with learned weights narrows the gap to strong ones. Download failed, so unread.
numbers: Not read this session; no numbers quoted.
limits: Unverified.
agent_relevance: Ensembles of diverse checks may beat one judge, but test against G4 on correlated errors.

source: Pitfalls of Rule- and Model-based Verifiers (reward hacking in RL with verifiable rewards)
finding: Rule-based verifiers reject correct answers in other formats; model-based verifiers can be fooled into false positives during RL. Download failed, so unread.
numbers: Not read this session; no numbers quoted.
limits: Unverified.
agent_relevance: Normalise answer formats in code; do not use a model verifier as the only reward.
